topic: The self grading problem in AI agent ROI

tweets.text: Your AI agent's ROI slide says 91 percent resolved and 40 percent cost cut. Before that goes near a board, ask one question. Who graded this number?
tweets.headline: Who Actually Graded Your ROI Number

tweets.text: In most rollouts, the same company running the agent also counts what it saved. That is not a scandal. It is just how these numbers get made.
tweets.headline: The Vendor Counts Its Own Savings

tweets.text: The vendor decides what counts as resolved. The vendor holds the raw logs. The vendor writes the number finance sees. No outside check in that chain.
tweets.headline: No Outside Check In That Chain

tweets.text: Most vendors are not hiding anything. Their dashboard honestly reflects how the system sees its own work. The problem is definitional, not dishonest.
tweets.headline: Honest Dashboard, Wrong Definition

tweets.text: But a system that scores its own homework gets to pick the easiest honest definition of success. Over a few release cycles, that definition drifts.
tweets.headline: Self Scored Metrics Drift One Way

tweets.text: Nobody decides one day to inflate the metric. It happens through a hundred small, reasonable choices, each one defensible on its own.
tweets.headline: A Hundred Small Reasonable Choices

tweets.text: Choice one. Count a ticket resolved the moment the agent stops responding, before anyone confirms the customer is actually satisfied.
tweets.headline: Resolved Before Anyone Confirms Satisfaction

tweets.text: Choice two. Measure against tickets routed to the agent, not total support volume. That quietly shrinks the denominator.
tweets.headline: Shrinking The Denominator Inflates The Rate

tweets.text: Choice three. Treat a human correction as a successful handoff instead of a failure the agent should be charged for.
tweets.headline: Corrections Counted As Successful Handoffs

tweets.text: Stack all three together and the number moves in exactly one direction. Nobody doing the counting has a reason to notice. 👀
tweets.headline: Nobody Counting Has A Reason To Notice

tweets.text: This is the same reason audited financial statements exist. Not because every company lies about revenue.
tweets.headline: Why Audited Financial Statements Exist

tweets.text: Self assessment has a built in direction of error, and that direction is always flattering. Finance figured this out decades ago. 📊
tweets.headline: Self Assessment Always Flatters Itself

tweets.text: So why does an AI agent savings number get a pass that revenue never would? It is often the biggest number on the slide.
tweets.headline: The Biggest Number Gets No Audit

tweets.text: A verified number needs three things most vendor dashboards skip. First, a definition of resolved fixed before measurement starts, not after.
tweets.headline: Fix The Definition Before You Measure

tweets.text: Second, access to the raw session log, not just the rolled up percentage. If nobody outside the vendor can check the claim, it is not a check.
tweets.headline: Raw Logs Beat Rolled Up Percentages

tweets.text: Third, a record of what changed in the methodology between quarters. A jump should trace to better performance, not a quieter definition change.
tweets.headline: Track What Changed Between Quarters

tweets.text: None of this means distrusting the team running the agent. It means treating the ROI number the way finance treats every other number on that slide.
tweets.headline: Treat ROI Like Every Other Number

tweets.text: Every other figure in the deck has a source trail. The AI savings line is usually the one exception, and often the loudest number in the room. 🎯
tweets.headline: The One Line Without A Source Trail

tweets.text: If your board asks who counted the resolution rate and the honest answer is the vendor who built the product, that is the gap to close.
tweets.headline: Ask Who Actually Counted The Resolution

tweets.text: That is exactly why we built agentworth. An independent audit log of what your agent actually did, so the ROI number does not grade its own homework. 💡
tweets.headline: An Independent Audit Log For Agents
